title: Four Reasons That I'm Ready and Excited for Year 15 of Teaching
author: The Broken Copier
summary: In a reflective back-to-school essay, a veteran teacher writing as The Broken Copier frames the start of a fifteenth year of teaching through Zadie Smith's White Teeth, using its meditation on consequence and unpredictability to argue that teaching's defining feature is its irreducible lack of precision. The author lays out four concrete reasons for entering the new year with enthusiasm: building a student-reflection system separate from high-stakes assessment, teaching Frankenstein for the first time after years of King Lear, using a self-authored goal-setting template rather than an administrative form, and simply welcoming the unpredictability of a new cohort. The piece closes with a pointed rebuttal of the Alpha School model via Carl Hendrick's variance argument, using teacher-quality variance as evidence that good teaching resists standardization and packaging. Throughout, the essay treats variance and unpredictability not as problems to be engineered away but as the source of teaching's meaning, positioning that stance against a broader educational culture chasing spreadsheet-friendly precision.
points: Uses a literary frame (Zadie Smith's White Teeth and the Samad-Archie exchange on consequence) to argue that teaching's value lies precisely in its unpredictability, not despite it - a direct counter to standardization-minded reform culture.

Builds a concrete, non-assessment reflection system (photographed notebook moments compiled into an ongoing document) explicitly designed to surface a teacher's own understanding of student learning, not just the students'.
Treats curriculum choice - swapping a well-worn King Lear unit for a first-time Frankenstein unit based on direct student feedback - as a marker of professional agency worth naming and defending.

Deploys Carl Hendrick's 'you can't scale good teaching' argument and its teacher-quality-variance evidence as a direct rebuttal to Alpha School-style scaling claims, framing variance in teaching quality as a feature to protect rather than an inefficiency to standardize away.
Reframes 'I'm ready for this school year' as a decision to actively author one's own goals and curriculum choices rather than default to generic, imposed planning templates.
quotes: Every little trifle, for some reason, does seem incalculably important today. There's never any knowing which of our actions, which of our idlenesses won't have things hanging on it for ever.
On cold days a man can see his breath, on a hot day he can't. On both occasions, the man breathes. On both occasions, the teacher teaches.

It feels as if we are in a moment in education that is desperate for precision, for a technocratic, spreadsheet-friendly way to measure each and every smidgeon of learning. The inescapable lack of precision, while without question the most infuriating part of this work, is also without question the most beautiful part of this work.
Classrooms are better when teachers can make more choices within them, and I cannot wait to see what happens with this one.

You have massive variance in teacher quality and pupil outcomes in a way that most people would find shocking, he says. The variance within schools between teacher quality is often greater than the variance between schools. If you apply that to doctors or dentists, there'd be a public outcry.
Good teaching has looked different every single year of my career. That variance is a beautiful thing, something worth affirming and celebrating.

It makes me sad that there are those who want to stifle it, to try and package it into a box and market it to the masses. But it also makes me ready and excited to step back into the classroom to begin Year 15, because that is where the work is, beautifully and imperfectly and meaningfully.
